title: $30,000 a Year Is How Much an Hour? (2026)
metaDescription: $30,000 a year is $14.42/hour at 40 hrs/week — $576.92 weekly, $2,500 monthly. Full 2026 breakdown with a federal take-home estimate.

hero.lede: Based on a 40-hour week worked 52 weeks a year (2,080 hours). Below: every pay-period equivalent, the rate at other workweeks, a 2026 federal take-home estimate, and how $30,000 compares with the U.S. median.

shortAnswer.heading: How much is $30,000 a year per hour?
shortAnswer.html: $30,000 a year is $14.42 an hour at 40 hours a week, 52 weeks a year (2,080 hours). That's $115.38 a day, $576.92 a week, $1,153.85 biweekly, and $2,500.00 a month — all gross. After estimated federal income tax and FICA, a single filer keeps about $26,285 a year, roughly $2,190 a month.

sections.title: What $30,000 looks like per paycheck.
sections.note: All figures are gross (pre-tax). See the take-home table below for the federal-only estimate after taxes.

sections.title: Where $30,000 stands in 2026.
paragraphs: A salary of $30,000 works out to $14.42 an hour on the standard full-time schedule — 40 hours a week for all 52 weeks, or 2,080 paid hours a year. Employers quote pay by the year, but bills arrive by the month, so the number that matters for planning is usually $2,500.00 of gross pay per month.

That sits about 54% below the U.S. median. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports median weekly earnings of $1,251 for full-time workers (BLS, Q2 2026), which annualizes to roughly $65,052. Keep in mind that cost of living moves the goalposts — the same $30,000 stretches very differently in a high-rent metro than in a lower-cost region, even though the hourly math is identical.

sections.title: The hourly rate depends on your hours.
sections.note: Salaried roles rarely pay overtime — at 45 hours a week the same $30,000 effectively pays $12.82 per hour worked.

sections.title: From $30,000 gross to take-home.
sections.note: Single filer, standard deduction, no state/local income tax, no credits or pre-tax benefits. Your actual paycheck will differ.

sections.title: Why the 12% bracket doesn't mean 12% tax.
paragraphs: Start with the $16,100 standard deduction for a single filer in 2026: it shields the first slice of income, leaving $13,900 federally taxable. That tops out in the 12% bracket — but the bracket overstates the bite. Total federal income tax comes to $1,420, an effective rate of just 4.7%, plus $2,295 in Social Security and Medicare.

Net of federal income tax and FICA, expect about $26,285 a year, or $2,190.42 monthly (12.4% total federal withholding). Applied to the classic 50/30/20 framework, that funds roughly $1,095 of needs, $657 of wants, and $438 of monthly saving — state taxes, where they apply, come out of this too.

faq.q: How much is $30,000 a year per hour?
faq.a: $30,000 a year is $14.42 an hour at 40 hours a week (2,080 hours a year). At 37.5 hours a week it rises to $15.38 an hour, and if you actually work 45-hour weeks it averages $12.82 per hour worked.

faq.q: How much is $30,000 a year biweekly?
faq.a: Gross biweekly pay on $30,000 is $1,153.85 ($30,000 ÷ 26 pay periods). After estimated federal income tax and FICA for a single filer, roughly $1,010.96 per check remains — before state taxes and benefits.

faq.q: How much is $30,000 a year after taxes?
faq.a: Using 2026 federal brackets and the $16,100 standard deduction, a single filer earning $30,000 pays about $1,420 in federal income tax and $2,295 in FICA, keeping roughly $26,285 a year ($2,190.42 a month). This is a federal-only estimate — state and local taxes reduce it further.

$30,000 is about 54% below the U.S. median full-time salary of roughly $65,052 (BLS, Q2 2026: $1,251/week). Whether it is "good" depends heavily on your metro's cost of living, household size, and debt load — the same salary goes much further in a low-cost region than in an expensive coastal city.

faq.q: What tax bracket is $30,000 in for 2026?
faq.a: After the $16,100 standard deduction, $30,000 leaves $13,900 of taxable income, which puts a single filer in the 12% marginal bracket for 2026. Only income above each threshold is taxed at the higher rate, so the effective federal rate is just 4.7%.

methodology: Conversions are straight arithmetic on gross salary: $30,000 ÷ 2,080 hours (40 × 52) for hourly, ÷ 260 workdays for daily, ÷ 52, 26, 24 and 12 for the pay-period figures. No taxes are applied to those rows.

The take-home estimate uses 2026 federal brackets for a single filer with the $16,100 standard deduction, plus employee FICA (6.2% Social Security + 1.45% Medicare). It excludes state/local income tax, credits, and pre-tax benefits such as 401(k) or health premiums — so real paychecks will differ.
The median comparison uses BLS median usual weekly earnings for full-time wage and salary workers: $1,251/week (BLS, Q2 2026).
Educational estimates only — not tax, legal, or financial advice.
